1: In Rājagaha, a rich merchant’s daughter became intimate with a servant. Afraid of being found out, they took their valuables, went out by the main gate and left for a distant land.
2: Both their sons were born on the road, so they were called Panthaka, “Road”: the elder Mahāpanthaka, the younger Cūḷapanthaka.
3: When she brought the boys to Rājagaha, her parents would not see her; they sent money and asked only for the children. The boys grew up in their grandfather’s house.
4: The elder, Mahāpanthaka, was drawn to the Buddha’s teaching, went forth, and in time became an arahant.
5: At his brother’s urging Cūḷapanthaka also went forth, but after four months he still could not learn a single verse.
6: His elder brother, who was in charge of the meals, said, “You are unfit for this teaching. Leave here,” and sent him out of the monastery.
7: When Jīvaka the physician came to the Mango Grove and invited the monks to a meal, the elder brother accepted for all except his younger brother.
8: At dawn Cūḷapanthaka set out to return to lay life, but the Buddha was waiting for him on the road.
9: The Buddha gave him a clean piece of cloth made by psychic power, and told him to sit facing east, rubbing it and repeating, “Removal of impurity.”
10: Seeing the clean cloth grow dirty as he rubbed it, he saw impermanence. At the end of the Buddha’s verses he became an arahant.
11: At Jīvaka’s house, as water was poured, the Buddha covered the vessel with his hand and said, “A monk remains in the monastery.”
12: The messenger went to the Mango Grove and found it filled with a thousand monks, created by Cūḷapanthaka’s psychic power.
13: He called, “Cūḷapanthaka!” and a thousand voices answered. When he took the first one by the hand, the others vanished.
14: After the meal, at the Buddha’s request, Cūḷapanthaka gave Jīvaka a teaching in thanksgiving.
15: That evening the monks were praising the Buddha in the Dhamma hall. The Buddha came and told them a story of the past.
16: Long ago in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a treasurer called Cūḷaseṭṭhi. Seeing a dead mouse in the road, he said, “A sharp young man could support a wife and start a business with this.”
17: A poor young man who heard him picked up the dead mouse.
18: He sold the mouse as food for a cat and received one kākaṇikā, the smallest coin.
19: With it he bought molasses and gave it with water to flower-gatherers coming home from the forest. They gave him flowers, and selling them he earned eight kahāpaṇas.
20: After a great storm filled the king’s garden with fallen branches, he offered to clear it all if he could keep the wood.
21: He gave molasses to the children at play and had them pile the branches at the garden gate.
22: The king’s potter bought the firewood, giving him sixteen kahāpaṇas and five vessels such as water-jars. Now he had twenty-four kahāpaṇas.
23: At the city gate he gave water to five hundred grass-cutters, and they promised to help him.
24: When a horse-dealer arrived with five hundred horses, he sold him five hundred bundles of grass for a thousand kahāpaṇas.
25: When a great ship came into port, he hired a carriage for eight kahāpaṇas, went to the harbour, left his signet ring as a deposit and bought the cargo.
26: A hundred merchants who came for the cargo each paid him a thousand kahāpaṇas twice over, and he gained two hundred thousand.
27: He took a hundred thousand kahāpaṇas to Cūḷaseṭṭhi to thank him, and told him the whole story, beginning with the dead mouse.
28: Cūḷaseṭṭhi, not wanting to lose so wise a young man, gave him his daughter in marriage.
29: When Cūḷaseṭṭhi passed away, the young man took over the treasurer’s position in that city.
30: The Buddha spoke the verse: “As one fans a tiny spark into a fire, the wise rise up from small means.” “The young man was Cūḷapanthaka, and Cūḷaseṭṭhi was I myself.”
